title: Fewest Treats for a Rated Line
statement:
Children stand in a line, and ratings[i] is the score of child i. You hand out treats under two rules:

  • Every child gets at least one treat.
  • A child with a strictly higher rating than a neighbour standing directly next to them gets more treats than that neighbour.

Neighbours with equal ratings have no rule between them. Return the smallest total number of treats that satisfies both rules.

examples.why: Treats 3, 2, 1, 2. The falling run 4 > 3 > 2 forces the first child up to 3, even though nobody to their left needs that.
Treats 1, 2, 1. The two children rated 2 are equal, so the last one can drop back to 1.
Treats 1, 2, 3, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1. The peak needs 4 from the left slope but 5 from the longer right slope, and must take the larger.

hints: Each rule involves only a left neighbour or a right neighbour. Can you satisfy each direction separately?
Pass left to right: if a child beats the left neighbour, give them one more than that neighbour, else 1. This fixes every "left" rule. Then do the same from right to left.
In the second pass, do not overwrite: take the maximum of what the child already has and one more than the right neighbour, so the left rule stays satisfied.

explain.intuition:
The rule for a child points two ways: compared with the left neighbour and with the right one. Handle the directions separately. A left-to-right pass gives each child the least it needs to beat its left neighbour: one more than the left neighbour on a rise, otherwise 1. That is the length of the rising run ending at it. A right-to-left pass computes the same thing for falling runs.

The true minimum for each child is the larger of the two numbers. It has to be at least each of them, and taking the maximum never breaks a rule that the other pass had already fixed, because raising a child's count only makes it harder for its neighbours to beat it, and they only need to beat it if they are rated higher, in which case they were also raised by the same pass. Summing the maxima gives the smallest total.
steps: Create left filled with 1. For i from 1 to n − 1: if ratings[i] > ratings[i − 1], set left[i] = left[i − 1] + 1.
Walk from the right with a running value right = 1 for the last child. For i from n − 2 down to 0: if ratings[i] > ratings[i + 1], right grows by 1, else it resets to 1.
Add max(left[i], right) to the total for every child.
pitfalls: Giving a child more because the neighbour has an equal rating. Equal neighbours have no rule.
Doing only one pass, which misses falling runs like the first example.
In the second pass, setting the value to right instead of taking the maximum, which breaks the left rule at peaks.

solutions.title: Fix violations until nothing changes
solutions.idea: Start everyone at 1 and keep sweeping, bumping any child who should beat a neighbour but does not, until a sweep changes nothing.

solutions.title: Two passes, take the maximum
solutions.idea: One pass satisfies every left-neighbour rule, the other every right-neighbour rule. Each child needs the larger of the two.

followups: Solve it in O(1) extra space by counting the lengths of rising and falling slopes in a single pass.
The children stand in a circle instead of a line. What breaks, and how do you fix it?
